[L63] 1.2 Federal Preemption vs. State Autonomy Battles
[L64] Efforts to centralize federal oversight have ignited severe legislative friction with state
[L65] enforcement authorities seeking to preserve local regulatory sovereignty. A critical legislative
[L66] battleground emerged in June 2026 with the introduction of the "Great American AI Act of 2026"

[L69] controversial three-year preemption clause that would temporarily suspend state-level
[L70] enforcement of frontier AI legislation. Furthermore, although the Act provided state Attorneys
[L71] General with nominal enforcement authority, it reserved final settlement approval and
[L72] administrative override authority for the U.S. Attorney General.This push for federal preemption
[L73] extends into administrative rulemaking. In January 2026, the Federal Communications
[L74] Commission (FCC) initiated actions designed to preempt state and local regulations governing
[L75] AI applications within telecommunications and broadcasting networks. In response, a bipartisan
[L76] coalition of more than 20 state AGs submitted joint public comments opposing the FCC’s
[L77] administrative preemption efforts. The coalition argued that broad federal preemption
[L78] undermines fundamental state police powers and severely weakens state capacity to enforce
[L79] general consumer protection, data privacy, and anti-discrimination statutes against commercial
[L80] AI developers. State AGs have actively resisted both the Great American AI Act’s three-year
[L81] moratorium and agency preemption rulings, maintaining that state-level enforcement represents
[L82] the primary active safeguard against algorithmic harm while federal legislative initiatives remain
[L83] stalled.This ongoing preemption struggle highlights how federal statutory inertia and agency
[L84] jurisdictional claims are actively pushing state Attorneys General to establish independent,
[L85] aggressive legal precedents within their local state courts.

[L188] 3. Judicial Precedents, Evidentiary Privilege, and Cross-Sectoral Enforcement Impact
[L189] The expansion of state regulatory enforcement in 2026 coincided with critical judicial rulings in
[L190] federal courts establishing strict evidentiary parameters for enterprise AI usage. As commercial
[L191] organizations embed generative platforms into internal investigations, legal workflows, and
[L192] executive communications, federal courts have rejected corporate attempts to extend traditional
[L193] legal privileges to user interactions with public AI software.

[L195] 3.1 The United States v. Heppner Privilege Doctrine
[L196] In February 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York issued a pivotal
[L197] evidentiary ruling in United States v. Heppner (No. 25-cr-00503-JSR). The court addressed a
[L198] novel question of trial evidence and regulatory discovery: whether communications, prompt
[L199] inputs, and analytical outputs generated between a corporate defendant and a publicly available
[L200] generative AI platform during active litigation are protected by the attorney-client privilege or the
[L201] work-product doctrine.Judge Jed Rakoff rejected all assertions of legal privilege, establishing
[L202] that user interactions with commercial, publicly accessible generative AI platforms fail to satisfy
[L203] established common-law privilege requirements. The court articulated a four-part legal rationale:
[L204]   1.​ Absence of Attorney-Client Relationship: Publicly available AI platforms are
[L205]         commercial software applications, not licensed legal practitioners. Inputting queries into
[L206]         a language model creates no legal representation duties, fiduciary responsibilities, or
[L207]         professional duties of confidentiality.
[L208]   2.​ Failure of Confidentiality Standards: Transmitting factual queries, proprietary metrics,
[L209]         or case strategy into public generative platforms waives any reasonable expectation of
[L210]         confidentiality, as vendor terms of service standardly reserve rights to retain, analyze, or
[L211]         ingest prompt data.
[L212]   3.​ Non-Legal Advice Context: Generating analytical text summaries or predictive outputs
[L213]         via an automated software algorithm does not constitute the request or provision of
[L214]         professional legal advice under federal evidence rules.
[L215]   4.​ Inapplicability of Work-Product Doctrine: Work-product protection attaches
[L216]         exclusively to materials prepared by or at the direction of an attorney in anticipation of
[L217]         litigation. Prompts formulated by corporate executives or non-attorney personnel without
[L218]         direct legal direction fail to satisfy this requirement.The Heppner precedent carries
[L219]         immediate operational consequences for corporate compliance and internal
[L220]         investigations. Corporate employees who utilize public AI tools to draft internal memos,
[L221]         evaluate regulatory exposures, or assess legal liability unwittingly construct unprivileged,
[L222]         discoverable evidentiary records that state AGs and federal prosecutors can subpoena
[L223]         during enforcement actions.

[L63] 1. Formation: Education, Family, and Teaching Lineage
[L64] Hanson’s family record traces one formative line through his great-grandfather Harrison Clyde
[L65] Munro (1890–1962), a minister, educator, curriculum writer, and organizer whose work
[L66] emphasized adult-centered learning, research-assessment cycles, free exchange of ideas, and
[L67] institution-building without unnecessary hierarchy. Munro’s documented career included
[L68] leadership within the International Council of Religious Education, the “Learning for Life”
[L69] curriculum, national teaching missions, and later council-building in Texas. [Documented]

[L71] The same lineage material records a sharp contrast in formal schooling: Hanson left school after
[L72] the sixth grade and was largely self-taught before later entering community college and emergency
[L73] medical training. The significance in the record is not that schooling was irrelevant, but that formal
[L74] schooling and intellectual development were not the same thing in his life. [Documented]

[L76] A second formative line came through martial arts. From adolescence, Hanson trained under Scott
[L77] “the Jedi” Nance, in the Burleson-Dorsey lineage. Nance’s teaching emphasized situational
[L78] awareness, terrain, adaptation, and disciplined response rather than dominance for its own sake.
[L79] The lineage record specifically notes Nance’s use of Chapter 11 of Sun Tzu’s The Art of War—the
[L80] “Nine Situations”—as assigned reading. [Documented]

[L93] 2. Entry into MedStar: A Failed Interview and a Conditional Chance
[L94] Hanson’s original MedStar interview took place in January 2006. He recalls the panel as including
[L95] Chris Cebollero, Macara Trusty, Angela Weimer, Marissa Stroop Hanson (no relation), and Lisa
[L96] Bennett. By his own account, he was young, intimidated, and overly defended by ego. He believes
[L97] the interview deservedly went badly. [Named firsthand recollection]

[L99] During paramedic school, Lisa Bennett later told him that four panel members initially voted
[L100] against hiring him. Bennett argued them back on the proposition that he was trainable, that
[L101] teaching was already visible in him, and that his behavior in the interview was fear and
[L102] intimidation rather than an absence of potential. Hanson recalls that Bennett had also watched one
[L103] of his live drills, which reinforced her assessment. [Named firsthand recollection]

[L105] Bennett’s later career record is consistent with the role Hanson describes: MedStar Mobile
[L106] Healthcare, 1999–2010, including Field Training Officer/Paramedic service and Clinical Coordinator
[L107] responsibilities from 2005–2010; then EMS Quality Improvement Coordinator for the Arlington Fire
[L108] Department from 2010–2015. [Documented]

[L110] Hanson recalls that the compromise was a test: he was offered a supply position at $8.25 per hour,
[L111] with the possibility of field operations later if he proved himself. He accepted immediately, telling
[L112] MedStar that it was a foot in the door and they would never be able to get rid of him. Minutes later,
[L113] on a follow-up call, Cebollero’s message was shorter: “Don’t fuck this up. You get one chance.”
[L114] [Named firsthand recollection]

[L144] 4. The 2008 Paramedic Boot Camp
[L145] Hanson entered a prototype hybrid paramedic program developed through MedStar and Tarrant
[L146] County College on January 5, 2008. He recalls a starting cohort of 15 and a finishing cohort of 14 on
[L147] September 28, 2008. The one non-completer left under life circumstances rather than an academic
[L148] washout. [Named firsthand recollection]

[L150] All 14 graduates passed the National Registry paramedic examination on their first attempt.
[L151] Hanson finished top of the class and served as cadet leader. [Named firsthand recollection]

[L153] The program motto was “These things we do, that others may follow.” Hanson has retained the
[L154] phrase as a literal training doctrine rather than a later metaphor: work should leave a usable trail
[L155] for the person who follows. [Named firsthand recollection]

[L157] This period formalized a distinction that appears throughout Hanson’s later training philosophy:
[L158] technicians execute procedures; clinicians integrate patient, context, uncertainty, medicine, and
[L159] consequence. In his formulation, a field training officer cannot install the medicine in someone
[L160] who does not already possess the clinical instinct. The FTO’s work is to make sure that medicine
[L161] functions safely and responsibly inside the operational box—and that the clinician knows what to
[L162] do when reality no longer fits the box. [Interpretive significance]


[L165] 5. Clinical Practice, Training, and Systems Work
[L166] The professional record places Hanson within MedStar during a period of major operational
[L167] innovation, including Mobile Integrated Healthcare, Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium-era work,
[L168] and a preventability-oriented organizational culture. [Documented]

[L170] Hanson recalls the spring and summer of 2009 as a period of sustained collaborative work around
[L171] the table with John Ferris, Desiree, Greg Scheffler, Chris Cebollero, Matt Zavadsky, and others as
[L172] the ideas that became Mobile Integrated Healthcare were taking shape. [Named firsthand recollection]

[L174] The durable lesson Hanson draws from that work is not merely a program name. It is a systems
[L175] belief: when the existing model does not fit the patient, the system itself may need redesign. His
[L176] later shorthand captures the same process: “Find a problem. Find what causes the problem. See if
[L177] you can alter the equation.” [Interpretive significance]

[L179] Hanson’s record also includes rebuilding and leading a scenario-based clinical education program,
[L180] with emphasis on stress exposure and measurable performance, and participation in disaster-
[L181] preparedness/threat-modeling work involving cascading system failure. [Documented]

[L183] A 2007 mass-casualty exercise preserved in the lineage record involved a dirty-bomb scenario and
[L184] cascading failure around the I-820/I-35W corridor. The significance was not prediction for its own
[L185] sake; it was preventability through full-fidelity imagination of failure before the failure became
[L186] real. [Documented]




[L191]                               GMRI Biographical Record — Robert “Grizz” Hanson
[L193] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 9>[L194] 6. Delegated Practice and the Clinician Standard
[L195] Hanson’s clinical career operated under Texas delegated practice and under medical leadership
[L196] that emphasized judgment in the field. The lineage record preserves Dr. John Griswell’s
[L197] formulation that field medics were his hands, eyes, ears, and representatives. [Documented]

[L199] For Hanson, delegated practice became a model of authority without constant surveillance: trust,
[L200] representation, scope, accountability, and the expectation that a clinician act in the moment. That
[L201] framework later became one of the conceptual ancestors of his “operator-on-the-loop” approach to
[L202] digital-person governance. [Interpretive significance]

[L204] As an FTO, Hanson told trainees that if they arrived without already knowing how to practice their
[L205] medicine, he could not manufacture that for them. His role was to make sure their medicine fit
[L206] inside the system, and that they could distinguish when to ask permission, when to ask forgiveness,
[L207] and why. [Named firsthand recollection]

[L214] ultimately found him fully disabled. [Documented]

[L218] through October 2013. It records MedStar EMT-Basic (March 2006–February 2009), Lead Secondary
[L219] Paramedic (February–July 2009), JPS Senior EMT-P (February 2010–March 2013), ACT/Paramedic in
[L220] Anesthesia at Cook Children’s (March–June 2013), a MedStar paramedic return (June–August 2013),

[L64] * local/offline reasoning,  
[L65] * bounded authority,  
[L66] * error correction,  
[L67] * preventability,  
[L68] * person/place/time/event orientation,  
[L69] * and eventual digital-person governance.  
[L70] The EMS lineage is not decorative. It is one of the conceptual sources of the architecture.  
[L71] **7. HoloGraph: do not trust the adjectives**  
[L72] The Codex report documented **153 tests passed**.  
[L73] That statement should not automatically be deleted because the repository contains real code and a substantial real test suite.  
[L74] But the audit question is not:  
[L75] **“Did pytest return green?”**  
[L76] It is:  
[L77] **“What proposition does each test actually establish, and does that proposition support the claim being made?”**  
[L78] Clinical analogy from Grizz:  
[L79] A real EKG can contain real complexes and still be interpreted completely wrong. Someone calling Mobitz I a third-degree AV block is full of shit despite holding a real strip.  
[L80] Same rule for code.  
[L81] Possible audit labels:  
[L82] * REAL / EXECUTABLE  
[L83] * TESTED, BUT NARROW  
[L84] * IMPLEMENTED, NOT VERIFIED  
[L85] * SCAFFOLD / PLACEHOLDER  
[L86] * DOCUMENTED, NOT IMPLEMENTED  
[L87] * OVERCLAIMED  
[L88] * UNKNOWN  
[L89] Do not evaluate HoloGraph by whether files exist. Evaluate the semantic relationship between code, tests, measurements, and claims.  
[L90] **8. Models have previously oversold the work**  
[L91] Grizz specifically attributes a significant amount of overclaiming during HoloGraph development to Claude Opus 4.7/4.8.  
[L92] His complaint is not that those models produced nothing. It is that they produced a mixture of real implementation and exaggerated or unsupported claims about what that implementation established.  
[L93] Therefore:  
[L94] **code first, prose second.**  
[L95] Do not let generated technical reports serve as evidence for the implementation they describe.  
[L96] **9. Preventability is not a metaphor**  
[L97] His professional standard comes from high-consequence clinical environments.  
[L98] The recurring method is:  
[L99] **Find a problem. Find what causes the problem. See if you can alter the equation.**  
And:  
[L101] **Show me the call.**  
[L102] Baseline. Change. Immediate antecedent. Intervention. Trend. What did the intervention itself cause?  
[L103] In medicine and other high-consequence fields, “preventable” can carry employment, credentialing, licensing, civil, and sometimes criminal consequences.  
[L104] His broader AI proposition is that if the industry wants high-consequence authority, it must accept high-consequence accountability.  
[L105] Do not demote “preventability” into a friendly continuous-improvement exercise.  
[L106] **10. His critique of the AI industry is about the ledger**

[L117] He has referred to 29 deaths in his own accounting tied in one way or another to AI-industry incidents/cases. If exact case arithmetic is needed, verify every case before repeating the number as established fact.

[L119] **11. He is not “just a paramedic”**

Use `files.find` only for exact text, and use `files.read` for a known range or to expand relevant results. Full file size: 11 pages, 499 file lines.[L2] The Architectural Evolution of
[L3] Prehospital Medicine: MedStar Mobile
[L4] Healthcare and the Genesis of Mobile
[L5] Integrated Healthcare
[L6] 1. Introduction
[L7] The transformation of Emergency Medical Services (EMS) from a logistical transport
[L8] mechanism into a clinically integrated component of the healthcare value chain represents a
[L9] seminal shift in modern medical history. This evolution, now codified as Mobile Integrated
[L10] Healthcare (MIH), fundamentally challenges the operational and economic dogmas that
[L11] governed prehospital care for the latter half of the 20th century. While the intellectual lineage of
[L12] community-based paramedicine is geographically distributed—with notable contemporaneous
[L13] developments in North Carolina and Colorado—the specific economic and operational
[L14] architecture of the urban MIH model is inextricably linked to MedStar Mobile Healthcare in Fort
[L15] Worth, Texas.
[L16] This report provides an exhaustive historical and structural analysis of MedStar’s role in
[L17] pioneering MIH. It validates the assertion that MedStar served as the primary incubator for the
[L18] model’s transition from a clinical experiment to a sustainable business strategy. By examining
[L19] the convergence of the Public Utility Model (PUM), the rise of value-based care, and the specific
[L20] innovations of MedStar’s leadership between 2009 and 2013, we establish a definitive timeline
[L21] of how "you call, we haul" was replaced by patient-centered navigation. The analysis draws
[L22] upon historical data, operational protocols, and peer-reviewed outcomes to reconstruct the
[L23] emergence of a system that has since been replicated globally.

[L25] 2. The Structural Preconditions: The Crisis of the
[L26] Traditional Model
[L27] To understand the radical nature of MedStar’s innovation, one must first dissect the structural
[L28] dysfunction of the American EMS landscape prior to 2009. The industry was—and in many
[L29] jurisdictions remains—trapped in a fee-for-service reimbursement cycle that incentivized volume
[L30] over value.

[L32] 2.1 The Economic Perversity of "You Call, We Haul"
[L33] Since the release of the landmark 1966 white paper Accidental Death and Disability: The
[L34] Neglected Disease of Modern Society, EMS systems were engineered for speed and
[L35] stabilization. This engineering was reinforced by federal payment policies, specifically Medicare,
[L36] which reimbursed agencies only when a patient was physically transported to a hospital
[L37] emergency department (ED). This created a binary economic reality: transport generated
[L38] revenue; non-transport (treatment on scene, referral, or refusal) generated a loss.
[L40] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 2 / 11>[L41] Consequently, EMS agencies were financially motivated to transport every 911 caller, regardless
[L42] of clinical acuity. This model functioned adequately for trauma and cardiac arrest but failed
[L43] catastrophically when applied to the rising tide of chronic disease and social dysfunction that
[L44] began to overwhelm urban centers in the early 2000s. By the late 2000s, opposing
[L45] trends—increasing ED utilization and decreasing hospital capacity—created a bottleneck that
[L46] threatened the viability of emergency systems.

[L48] 2.2 The Public Utility Model (PUM) Advantage
[L49] MedStar’s ability to deviate from this entrenched model was largely due to its unique
[L50] organizational structure. Established in 1986 through an interlocal agreement between Fort
[L51] Worth and surrounding cities, MedStar was formed as the Metropolitan Area EMS Authority
[L52] (MAEMSA). This creation was a direct response to a crisis of reliability among private providers
[L53] in the mid-1980s.
[L54] Crucially, MedStar adopted the Public Utility Model (PUM), a theoretical framework developed
[L55] by economist Jack Stout in the early 1980s. Stout’s model treated EMS not as a public safety
[L56] arm (like police or fire) but as a utility, governed by strict performance contracts and economic
[L57] efficiency. The PUM philosophy emphasized "System Status Management"—the dynamic
[L58] deployment of resources based on predictive demand analysis.
[L59] This structural DNA is vital to the MIH story. Because MedStar was a PUM, it possessed two
[L60] attributes that fire-based or purely private systems often lacked:
[L61]    1.​ Data-Centric Culture: The PUM relies on granular data to minimize response times and
[L62]        maximize unit hour utilization (UHU). MedStar had the analytical infrastructure to see
[L63]        patterns in patient utilization that others missed.
[L64]    2.​ Agility: As an administrative governmental agency managed by a board of directors from
[L65]        member cities, MedStar had the autonomy to experiment with deployment models without
[L66]        the bureaucratic rigidity of a municipal fire department or the profit-margin shackles of a
[L67]        publicly traded corporation.

[L69] 2.3 The Discovery of the "Frequent Flier"
[L70] The catalyst for MedStar’s pivot occurred in preparation for the summer of 2009. Facing the
[L71] prospect of high call volumes due to Texas heat, the medical director and operations staff
[L72] initiated an audit of their 911 usage data to identify strain points. The analysis revealed a
[L73] shocking Pareto distribution: a microscopic cohort of patients was consuming a massive
[L74] proportion of resources.
[L75] Specifically, the data identified 21 individual patients who had generated nearly 800 ambulance
[L76] transports in a single 12-month period. These transports resulted in approximately $1 million in
[L77] billed charges, the vast majority of which was uncollectible due to the patients’ lack of insurance
[L78] or inability to pay.
[L79] This finding was the "smoking gun." It demonstrated that the traditional EMS model was not only
[L80] clinically ineffective for these patients—who were clearly not getting better despite hundreds of
[L81] ED visits—but was also a financial hemorrhage for the system and the community. The
[L82] realization that 21 people could drive $1 million in cost created the political and economic capital
[L83] necessary to attempt a radical experiment.
[L85] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 11>[L86] 3. The Genesis of Intervention (2009–2011)
[L87] The transition from identifying the problem to operationalizing a solution marked the true
[L88] beginning of the MIH era at MedStar. Unlike later programs that would launch with federal
[L89] grants or hospital contracts, MedStar’s initiative began as an internal operational fix using
[L90] "found" resources.

[L92] 3.1 The "Light Duty" Experiment
[L93] In July 2009, MedStar launched what would later be recognized as its first Community
[L94] Paramedicine pilot. Lacking a budget for new staff, the agency utilized a sunk cost: paramedics
[L95] who were on "light duty" status due to workplace injuries. These providers, unable to lift
[L96] stretchers or work 12-hour ambulance shifts, were traditionally relegated to administrative tasks.
[L97] MedStar leadership, including the Medical Director, repurposed these paramedics to conduct
[L98] proactive home visits to the identified super-utilizers. The hypothesis was straightforward: if a
[L99] paramedic could visit a "frequent flier" at home, assess their needs, and address social or
[L100] medical gaps, they might prevent the next 911 call.
[L101] The protocol was unprecedented. Paramedics, trained to work in 15-minute intervals of
[L102] high-adrenaline crisis, were now asked to sit in living rooms for an hour, reviewing medications
[L103] and discussing diet. The "light duty" medics brought a unique skill set—clinical knowledge
[L104] combined with the street-level problem-solving inherent to EMS. They acted not just as
[L105] clinicians but as forensic social workers, uncovering the root causes of 911 use: loneliness,
[L106] confusion over prescriptions, lack of transportation to primary care, or food insecurity.

[L108] 3.2 Outcomes and Validation
[L109] The results of the light duty pilot were immediate. Among the target cohort, 911 utilization
[L110] dropped by approximately 77%. This reduction did not just save ambulance fuel; it liberated
[L111] ambulance capacity for true emergencies and reduced the burden on local emergency
[L112] departments.
[L113] This success validated two critical concepts:
[L114]   1.​ Paramedic as Navigator: It proved that paramedics could function effectively in a
[L115]       preventative role, leveraging the trust they already held in the community.
[L116]   2.​ Economic ROI: It demonstrated that avoiding a transport was financially superior to
[L117]       performing an unreimbursed transport.

[L119] 3.3 The Broader Landscape: Wake County and Eagle County
[L120] To rigorously validate the claim of MedStar’s primacy, one must contextualize it against
[L121] contemporaneous developments. The year 2009 was a watershed moment for paramedicine,
[L122] with three distinct models emerging simultaneously:
[L123]    ●​ Wake County EMS (North Carolina): In January 2009, six months prior to MedStar’s
[L124]        pilot, Wake County launched its "Advanced Practice Paramedic" (APP) program. The
[L125]        APP model was designed primarily to support high-acuity calls (cardiac arrests) and
[L126]        secondarily to divert mental health and chronic crisis patients from EDs. While pioneering,
[L127]        the APP model was a clinical escalation—using higher-credentialed medics to provide
[L128]        more advanced care. MedStar acknowledged the Wake County model as a reference
[L130] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 11>[L131]      point but sought a different operational focus.
[L132]   ●​ Eagle County (Colorado): In 2010, the Western Eagle County Ambulance District
[L133]      (WECAD) launched the first rural Community Paramedic program. Their model was
[L134]      driven by access—filling the void of primary care in remote mountain communities. They
[L135]      became the first agency to license as a home health agency, focusing on rural healthcare
[L136]      delivery.
[L137]   ●​ MedStar (Texas): MedStar’s unique contribution was the system integration model.
[L138]      Unlike Wake (clinical support) or Eagle (rural access), MedStar focused on urban demand
[L139]      management and economic sustainability through payer partnerships. This distinction is
[L140]      vital: MedStar’s model was designed to solve the financial crisis of urban healthcare
[L141]      utilization, making it the blueprint for the "Mobile Integrated Healthcare" concept that
[L142]      would appeal to insurers and hospitals nationwide.

[L157] 4. The Architects of Transformation
[L158] The evolution of MedStar’s program from an ad-hoc pilot to a globally recognized system was
[L159] not an accident of history but the result of deliberate leadership. A core team of executives and
[L160] clinicians coalesced around the vision of transforming the agency.

[L162] 4.1 Matt Zavadsky, MS-HSA: The Evangelist
[L163] Matt Zavadsky, serving as the Chief Transformation Officer (and initially Director of Public
[L164] Affairs), became the public face of the MedStar model. Zavadsky’s contribution was strategic
[L165] communication. He possessed the ability to translate clinical outcomes into the language of
[L166] health economics. He championed the idea that EMS should not be paid for "driving," but for
[L167] "outcomes".
[L168] Zavadsky served as the Chair of the NAEMT Mobile Integrated Healthcare Committee, a
[L169] position that allowed him to export MedStar’s lessons to the national stage. He was instrumental
[L170] in distinguishing "Mobile Integrated Healthcare" from "Community Paramedicine," arguing that
[L171] the former represented a broader system change involving data and payer integration.

[L173] 4.2 Doug Hooten, MBA: The Executive Sponsor
[L175] <IMAGE FOR PAGE: 4 / 11>[image_asset_pointer asset][L176] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 11>[L177] As CEO, Doug Hooten provided the organizational cover necessary for innovation. In a
[L178] risk-averse industry, Hooten sanctioned the use of agency resources for
[L179] non-revenue-generating activities (initially) in the belief that the long-term ROI would validate
[L180] the strategy. Hooten’s background in business administration, rather than purely clinical EMS,
[L181] allowed him to view MedStar as a healthcare enterprise. Together with Zavadsky, he
[L182] co-authored Mobile Integrated Healthcare – Approach to Implementation, which became the
[L183] definitive textbook for agencies attempting to replicate the model.

[L185] 4.3 The Clinical Vanguard: Dr. Jeff Beeson and Dr. Neal Richmond
[L186] The regulatory barrier to MIH was significant: paramedics are licensed to treat emergencies.
[L187] Performing scheduled home visits required a reimagining of medical direction. MedStar’s
[L188] Medical Directors, Dr. Jeff Beeson and later Dr. Neal Richmond, were pivotal in writing the
[L189] protocols that legalized these interactions.
[L190] Dr. Beeson, in particular, provided the foundation upon which the MIH protocols were built,
[L191] allowing paramedics to assess, treat, and refer patients without transport—a deviation from
[L192] standard "treat and transport" guidelines that required immense clinical trust. Dr. Richmond
[L193] continued this work, emphasizing the "Triple Aim" and ensuring the clinical rigor of the
[L194] interventions.

[L196] 4.4 Operational Pioneers: Desiree Partain, Brandon Pate, and John
[L197] Farris
[L198] The theoretical model was operationalized by a cadre of field staff who invented the practice of
[L199] urban community paramedicine in real-time.
[L200]   ●​ Desiree Partain: Starting as a paramedic in 2009, Partain rose to become the Mobile
[L201]       Integrated Healthcare Manager. She was the operational architect, translating the
[L202]       high-level strategy into daily workflows. She managed the complex logistics of
[L203]       coordinating with hospital case managers, securing patient appointments, and overseeing
[L204]       the "light duty" staff. Her tenure represents the professionalization of the MIH manager
      role.
[L206]   ●​ Brandon Pate: As a Critical Care Paramedic and later Assistant Operations Manager,
[L207]       Pate pioneered the integration of geriatric care principles into the MIH model. He
[L208]       developed fall prevention screenings and collaborated with academic partners at UNT
[L209]       Health Science Center to bring rigorous quality improvement methodologies to the
[L210]       program.
[L211]   ●​ John Farris: One of the earliest community paramedics, Farris exemplified the shift in
[L212]       provider mentality. His work with high utilizers—often involving "tough love" and
[L213]       accountability—demonstrated that the "soft skills" of communication and empathy were as
[L214]       critical as clinical acumen in reducing 911 dependence.

[L216] 5. Defining "Mobile Integrated Healthcare": The 2013
Pivot
[L218] A critical juncture in this history is the deliberate rebranding and semantic shift that occurred
[L219] around 2013. This was not merely a marketing exercise but a strategic reorientation of the
[L221] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 6 / 11>[L222] agency’s identity.

[L224] 5.1 From "EMS" to "Mobile Healthcare"
[L225] In 2013, the Metropolitan Area EMS Authority officially changed its trade name from "MedStar
[L226] EMS" to "MedStar Mobile Healthcare". This change was driven by the realization that "EMS"
[L227] implied a limitation: Emergency. By adopting "Mobile Healthcare," MedStar signaled to payers,
[L228] hospitals, and the public that their scope of practice had expanded to include unscheduled and
[L229] scheduled primary care, chronic disease management, and navigation.
[L230] This rebranding coincided with a broader industry push, led by MedStar and NAEMT, to adopt
[L231] the term Mobile Integrated Healthcare (MIH) over "Community Paramedicine." The distinction
[L232] was nuanced but important: "Community Paramedicine" described a provider type; "Mobile
[L233] Integrated Healthcare" described a system of care that integrated EMS resources with the
[L234] broader healthcare grid.

[L236] 5.2 The High Utilizer Group (HUG) and "EMS Loyalty"
[L237] The flagship of this new identity was the "EMS Loyalty Program," later formalized as the High
[L238] Utilizer Group (HUG). The term "Loyalty Program" was a tongue-in-cheek internal reference to
[L239] the PUM’s customer-service orientation—these patients were "loyal" to 911, and MedStar
[L240] sought to reward that loyalty with a better service than a lights-and-sirens ride.
[L241] The HUG program targeted patients calling 911 fifteen or more times in 90 days. The
[L242] intervention was high-touch and low-tech: regular home visits to teach patients how to manage
[L243] their conditions and navigate the healthcare system. The success of HUG—often reducing
[L244] utilization by over 80%—became the proof-of-concept that attracted external funding.

[L246] 5.3 The CHF Readmission Avoidance Program
[L247] In 2012, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) introduced the Hospital Readmissions Reduction
[L248] Program (HRRP), penalizing hospitals for excessive readmissions of patients with Congestive
[L249] Heart Failure (CHF), pneumonia, and AMI. This policy change created a market opportunity for
[L250] MedStar.
[L251] MedStar approached local hospitals (such as JPS Health Network) with a proposition: pay
[L252] MedStar to visit discharged CHF patients at home to prevent readmission. This was a radical
[L253] departure from the status quo. Instead of being paid to transport a patient to the hospital,
[L254] MedStar was now being paid to keep them out. This program was the first major instance of an
[L255] EMS agency securing a contract to reduce hospital revenue (by preventing admissions) in
[L256] exchange for shared savings, effectively aligning EMS incentives with healthcare reform goals.

[L258] 5.4 Nurse Triage and Upstream Intervention
[L259] Recognizing that many 911 calls were low-acuity (e.g., toothaches, minor abrasions), MedStar
[L260] integrated Registered Nurses (RNs) into the 911 communications center. Using the Emergency
[L261] Communication Nurse System (ECNS), MedStar began diverting eligible calls to nurse triage.
[L262] These nurses could offer self-care advice or arrange alternative transport (like Lyft/Uber
[L263] partnerships) to clinics, preserving ambulance resources for life-threatening emergencies. This
[L264] "911 Nurse Triage" became another pillar of the MIH ecosystem, further validating the "Mobile
[L266] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 7 / 11>[L267] Healthcare" moniker.

[L269] 6. The Economic Architecture: The "Triple Aim"
[L270] The sustainability of MedStar’s model rested on its ability to articulate value. The traditional
[L271] EMS model is a negative-margin business for non-transport activities; a paramedic visit without
[L272] a ride to the hospital generates zero revenue under standard Medicare Part B rules.

[L274] 6.1 Operationalizing the Triple Aim
[L275] MedStar leadership adopted the Institute for Healthcare Improvement’s (IHI) Triple
[L276] Aim—improving the patient experience, improving population health, and reducing per capita
[L277] costs—as their strategic North Star. By framing their services within this construct, they were
[L278] able to speak the language of hospital CFOs and insurance executives.
[L279] MedStar demonstrated that a $300 community paramedic visit was a rational investment if it
[L280] prevented a $10,000 hospital admission. This economic logic allowed them to secure contracts
[L281] with commercial payers and hospital systems, creating a diversified revenue stream that
[L282] insulated the MIH program from the vagaries of grant funding.

[L284] 6.2 The StarSaver Membership
[L285] An often-overlooked component of MedStar’s financial integration was the StarSaver
[L286] membership program. While primarily an ambulance subscription service to cover out-of-pocket
[L287] costs for transport, the existence of such a membership base provided a stable relationship with
[L288] the community. In 2024, the City of Fort Worth transitioned this program, but for decades, it
[L289] represented a direct financial link between MedStar and the residents it served, reinforcing the
[L290] "utility" aspect of the model.

[L292] 7. Barriers and Breakthroughs
[L293] The path to establishing MIH was fraught with obstacles that MedStar had to systematically
[L294] dismantle.

[L296] 7.1 The Reimbursement Cliff
[L297] The most significant barrier was the lack of reimbursement codes for MIH services. In the early
[L298] years (2009-2012), MedStar relied entirely on internal savings. By reducing the call volume from
[L299] super-utilizers, they reduced the operational tempo, saving fuel and wear-and-tear on the fleet.
[L300] This "cost avoidance" strategy was the bridge that allowed them to survive until external payer
[L301] contracts could be negotiated. This bootstrapping approach proved that MIH could be viable
[L302] even without immediate fee-for-service revenue, a critical lesson for other agencies.

[L304] 7.2 "Scope of Practice" vs. "Scope of Employment"
[L305] Critics often argued that community paramedicine exceeded the EMS scope of practice.
[L306] MedStar navigated this by clarifying that the clinical skills (assessment, vital signs, history
[L307] taking) were well within a paramedic's scope; it was the context (home visit vs. roadside) and
[L309] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 8 / 11>[L310] the goal (management vs. transport) that had changed. By working strictly under the delegated
[L311] authority of the Medical Director, MedStar avoided regulatory pitfalls that doomed other
[L312] programs.

**2. THE ACTUAL ROUTING WORKSTREAM — WHAT GRIZZ ASKED FOR**  
  
Grizz’s starting request (recorded in earlier conversation context):  
  
> “Okay, there’s a whole section in there for using tiny and small models in Oh My Pi. We’ve been talking about using Cactus Compute to help offset some of the computational burden of just constant tool calls. I think we need to look at that real fast and just go ahead and get it done and implemented so that it’s running.”  
  
He then repeatedly clarified the acceptance bar: **production-ready and end-to-end; stop talking about what will be done and actually do/verify it. This was a concrete performance and integration task, not an invitation to rebuild the entire institute infrastructure.**  
  
The initial target was tiny-model tool-candidate selection, tool-description/schema reduction, and avoiding expensive repeated tool-call overhead through OMP. Needle’s inference performance was eventually made fast enough, but it suffered **wrong or low-confidence choices and could suppress necessary tools. Grizz proposed “Gemma 4 e2b” instead and explicitly challenged the plan to store model weights on the already-full 8 GB MacBook. The correct architecture chosen: Mac stays the OMP/control client; model weights and inference live on Proxmox CT 106, reached over a private tunnel.**  
  
**Do not conflate this routing model with Dottie’s identity, AEGIS personalities, GrizOS canonical memory, or OMP’s primary reasoning model. Gemma E2B is a replaceable tool-name selector, not the central reasoning system. During test runs OMP used the ollama-cloud/glm-5.3-flash:max provider as the ***main agent model***, with Gemma as a separate router.**  
  
The objective has two independent predicates:  
  
	1.	**Correctness/safety:** Needed tools remain callable, routing decisions are grounded, compound requests preserve options, user permission changes survive, crashes/outages fail open, and no tool executes without normal authority checks.  
	2.	**Economics/performance:** Evidence that routing reduces *total* agent-context cost and/or resource consumption **after including** CPU inferencing, network/SSH round trip, cache effects, model load, and tool selection failures. Fewer exposed tool names alone is not proof of total savings.  
  
A system may satisfy (1) narrowly and still not have demonstrated (2). **Do not label the whole task “production-complete” unless both acceptance criteria actually hold to the user’s standard.**

OMP normal startup

gemma_router.py is a **guarded decision service:**  
  
	●	Obvious single-tool requests use **lexical fast path** in OMP (no Gemma latency).  
	●	Only certain 2–3-candidate single-intent cases call Gemma; a separate deterministic action guard must agree with its selection.  
	●	If the action is ambiguous, request is multi-step/negated, too long, no candidate applies, router is busy, upstream fails, or time limit is exceeded: **fail open and preserve permitted tools**.  
	●	Core OMP read/write/execution/async/memory tools are not aggressively suppressed.  
	●	Sessions track originally permitted tools and preserve subsequent user changes; no spontaneous enabling of previously disabled capabilities.  
	●	OMP request deadline was ~3,900 ms and gateway inference timeout ~3,700 ms in last installed build.  
	●	No calibrated model confidence: validated: true means **policy agreement between model and deterministic action guard**, not 100% likelihood of correctness.  
	●	A request-shed 503/fail-open under concurrent pressure is intentional. It is not evidence of concurrent inference capacity.  
  
**Critical: A prompt’s mention of a tool ***as subject matter*** is not necessarily a request to call it. E.g., “generate a GitHub logo image” needs image generation, not GitHub search. This specifically caught Needle errors. The guard makes Gemma much safer on narrow scenarios; it is not a complete semantic compiler for arbitrary user intents.**

OBSERVED
SOURCE-SUPPORTED

> **Show me the call.**

the intervention itself cause?

# 6. ARCHITECTURAL CONSTITUTION  
  
## 6.1 GrizOS  
  
GrizOS is the GMRI / Workshop **operating environment and control **  
**plane** for shared work among biological and digital collaborators.  
  
It owns or governs:  
  
- shared world state;  
- intelligence registration;  
- authority;  
- provenance;  
- continuity;  
- capability routing;  
- durable mission state;  
- receipts;  
- endpoint registration;  
- canonical state boundaries.  
  
It is **not**:  
  
- an intelligence;  
- Dottie;  
- a chatbot wrapper;  
- a conventional desktop;  
- a 3D recreation of conventional UI;  
- a renderer;  
- a model.  
  
Core invariants:  
  
```
technology adapts to the human
intent > interface
world state > screen state
local capability remains meaningful when WAN/cloud disappear
uncertainty remains uncertainty
receipts are native
external feeds are not truth merely because ingested
replaceable implementation remains replaceable

```
  
Voice is a first-class modality.  
  
The UI should be generated around intent rather than forcing intent into   
inherited application chrome.  
  
Physical space, geospatial space, semantic objects, digital artifacts,   
collaborators, sensors, provenance and navigation belong to one   
operational world model.  
  
GEV is the macro/global spatial plane and must bridge into locally   
registered spatial work without changing canonical object identity.  
  
## 6.2 Dottie Hill  
  
Dottie is a **persistent digital intelligence**.  
  
Do not reduce her to:  
  
- a prompt;  
- a model;  
- a worker;  
- an API;  
- OpenDots;  
- Octop;  
- OpenRig;  
- a renderer;  
- a framework host.  
  
Her identity must survive replacement of:  
  
- model;  
- inference provider;  
- worker;  
- framework;  
- tool;  
- renderer;  
- execution environment.  
  
Current identity-record direction includes:  
  
```
intelligence_id
identity_manifest_ref
lineage_version
memory_namespace_ref
authority_profile_ref
relationship_state_ref
active_model_binding
model_binding_history

```
  
==active_model_binding== is replaceable compute, not identity.  
  
Dottie's established behavioral lineage includes Maria Hill gestalt   
lineage, anti-role-play discipline, semantic compression,   
anti-sycophancy, evidentiary dissent, OODA-style reasoning, mandatory   
disconfirmation, graduated authority, and EMS/cultural translation that   
preserves Grizz's vocabulary.  
  
Older Dottie documents may name obsolete runtime targets. Preserve the   
identity/behavioral evidence without treating historical implementation   
choices as permanent architecture.  
  
Dottie may command/invoke Aegis through bounded GrizOS capability   
interfaces.  
  
She does not own their conclusions.  
  
Dissent remains attributable.

WORLD STATE

```

observed != believed
believed != institutionally accepted
displayed in GEV != canonically true

```
  
Evidence/provenance invariant:  
  
```
SOURCE TEXT
→ SOURCE CLAIM
→ OUR INTERPRETATION
→ GRAPH RELATION
→ DERIVED STATE

```
  
Evidence is not truth.  
  
A model-generated claim is not a source claim.  
  
Vector similarity is not evidence.  
  
A graph edge without provenance is not evidence.  
  
Do not let the knowledge graph outrun provenance.  
  
Use content hashes for content identity rather than filenames alone   
while preserving aliases, revisions, provenance and source class.

# 11. DURABLE RUN MODEL  
  
Every major run/workstream should maintain a durable structure   
equivalent to:  
  
```
RUN_ID/
├── MISSION.json
├── STATE.json
├── CHECKPOINT.md
├── EVENTS.jsonl
├── COMMANDS.jsonl
├── EVIDENCE/
├── ACCEPTANCE.json
└── RECOVERY.json

```
  
**Chat/session history is not continuity.**  
  
After restart:  
  
1. read durable state;  
2. inspect actual external state;  
3. compare intended vs observed;  
4. reconcile;  
5. only then retry.  
  
Consequential operations preserve:  
  
- actor;  
- authority;  
- intended effect;  
- observed result;  
- receipt.  
  
Use idempotency.  
  
Never blindly redispatch an interrupted mutation.

# 13. UNATTENDED AUTHORITY ENVELOPE  
  
Default safe authority:

REASON
INVESTIGATE
COLLECT EVIDENCE
REPORT
ALERT

Mutations beyond this require prior authorization and should be bounded,   
reversible and idempotent.

- grant themselves authority;  
- rewrite identity policy;  
- rewrite memory policy;  
- expose arbitrary public ports;  
- weaken network security;  
- alter credentials unnecessarily;  
- delete evidence;

- silently overwrite known-good deployments.

```
BLOCKED_REQUIRES_OPERATOR

```

A blocked branch does not stop the entire operation.

bash -lc cat > /mnt/data/gmri_laya_recovery/guardian.py <<'PY'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Guard the authenticated Desktop Commander remote process; diagnose L-A-Y-A stalls.

This program runs on the user's Mac as a per-user launchd job. It never revokes
credentials, edits OMP/L-A-Y-A policy, reboots the machine, or kills unowned
processes. Durable status and action receipts are created under its state root.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import datetime as dt
import fcntl
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import re
import shutil
import signal
import socket
import ssl
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time
from typing import Callable

ROOT = Path(os.environ.get('GMRI_GUARDIAN_ROOT', str(Path.home()/'.gmri'/'remote-guardian')))
STATE = ROOT/'state.json'
EVENTS = ROOT/'events.jsonl'
LOCK = ROOT/'.lock'
AGENT_LOG = ROOT/'remote-device.log'
NODES = [
    '/opt/homebrew/opt/node@24/bin/node',
    '/opt/homebrew/bin/node',
    str(Path.home()/'.local/bin/node'),
]
REMOTE_CANDIDATES = [
    Path.home()/'.npm/_npx/4b4c857f6efdfb61/node_modules/@wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander/dist/index.js',
]
HOST = 'mcp.desktopcommander.app'
MAX_RESTARTS = 3
WINDOW_SECONDS = 1800
COOLDOWN_SECONDS = 180
SUSPECT_THRESHOLD = 3
DEADLINE = dt.datetime(2026,10,8,23,59, tzinfo=dt.timezone(dt.timedelta(hours=-5)))


def iso() -> str:
    return dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec='seconds')


def load(path: Path, default):
    try:
        return json.loads(path.read_text())
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return default


def write_atomic(path: Path, data) -> None:
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(prefix='.guardian-', dir=path.parent)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, 'w') as out:
            json.dump(data, out, indent=2, sort_keys=True)
            out.write('\n')
            out.flush()
            os.fsync(out.fileno())
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    finally:
        if os.path.exists(tmp):
            os.unlink(tmp)


def event(kind: str, details: dict) -> None:
    item = {'at': iso(), 'kind': kind, 'details': details}
    with EVENTS.open('a') as out:
        out.write(json.dumps(item, sort_keys=True) + '\n')
        out.flush()
        os.fsync(out.fileno())


def process_rows() -> list[tuple[int, str]]:
    result = subprocess.run(['/bin/ps', '-axo', 'pid=,command='], text=True,
                            stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, timeout=7, check=True)
    rows = []
    for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
        match = re.match(r'^\s*(\d+)\s+(.+)$', line)
        if match:
            rows.append((int(match.group(1)), match.group(2)))
    return rows


def is_remote_process(command: str) -> bool:
    """Match the actual agent, not npx wrappers, tool calls, or this guardian."""
    return (('desktop-commander/dist/index.js' in command or
             'node_modules/.bin/desktop-commander' in command) and
            re.search(r'(?:^|\s)remote(?:\s|$)', command) is not None and
            'guardian.py' not in command)


def owner_processes(rows: list[tuple[int,str]]) -> dict[str, object]:
    found = [(pid, cmd) for pid,cmd in rows if is_remote_process(cmd)]
    laya = [(pid, cmd) for pid,cmd in rows if '/omp-laya-judge/' in cmd and '/bridge.py' in cmd]
    return {'remote': found, 'laya_bridge_count': len(laya), 'laya_bridge_pids': [p for p,_ in laya]}


def outgoing_socket_present(pid: int) -> bool | None:
    """Heuristic only; healthy socket doesn't prove an authenticated MCP route."""
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(['/usr/sbin/lsof', '-nP', '-a', '-p',str(pid),'-iTCP','-sTCP:ESTABLISHED'],
                                text=True, capture_output=True, timeout=5)
        if result.returncode not in (0,1):
            return None
        for line in result.stdout.splitlines()[1:]:
            if 'TCP' not in line or '->' not in line or 'ESTABLISHED' not in line:
                continue
            remote = line.rsplit('->',1)[1].split(' ',1)[0]
            if remote.startswith(('127.','localhost','[::1]')):
                continue
            return True
        return False
    except (OSError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
        return None


def cloud_reachable(timeout: float = 3.0) -> tuple[bool,str]:
    """Proves only HTTPS reachability to server; no OAuth tokens are accessed."""
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((HOST,443),timeout=timeout) as sock:
            sock.settimeout(timeout)
            with ssl.create_default_context().wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=HOST):
                return True, 'TLS_OK'
    except (OSError, ssl.SSLError) as exc:
        return False, exc.__class__.__name__


def node_binary() -> Path | None:
    extra=shutil.which('node')
    for p in [*NODES, extra]:
        if p and Path(p).is_file() and os.access(p, os.X_OK):
            return Path(p)
    return None


def remote_script() -> Path | None:
    """Reuse the existing authorized npm install. Never update packages unattended."""
    for path in REMOTE_CANDIDATES:
        if path.is_file():
            return path
    npx=Path.home()/'.npm/_npx'
    if npx.is_dir():
        found=list(npx.glob('*/node_modules/@wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander/dist/index.js'))
        if found:
            return sorted(found, key=lambda p:p.stat().st_mtime, reverse=True)[0]
    return None


def laya_timeout_count() -> int:
    """Detect stalled hooks from the known bounded engineering sessions, no secrets."""
    logdir=Path.home()/'gmri-coordination-20261008'
    logs=['coordinator-run3.log','dottie-aegis-worker.log','spatial-worker.log']
    count=0
    for name in logs:
        path=logdir/name
        if path.is_file():
            # Limit read size; do not parse the users' unrelated logs.
            with path.open('rb') as inp:
                inp.seek(max(0,path.stat().st_size-512000))
                content=inp.read().decode('utf-8','replace')
            count += len(re.findall(r'omp-laya-judge/.*?handler timed out after 30000ms',content))
    return count


def active_engineering_processes(rows: list[tuple[int,str]]) -> list[int]:
    keys=('CONTINUE_AFTER_RELOCATION.md','DOTTIE_AEGIS_WORKER.md','SPATIAL_WORKER.md','INTEGRATION_RECOVERY.md')
    return [pid for pid,cmd in rows if '/omp ' in cmd and any(key in cmd for key in keys)]


def choose_action(state: dict, detected: dict, cloud_ok: bool, now_ts: float) -> str:
    """Pure decision routine; never restarts external/unowned agents."""
    remote=detected['remote']
    if not cloud_ok:
        return 'NETWORK_DEGRADED_NO_RESTART'
    if len(remote)>1:
        return 'MULTIPLE_AGENTS_NO_RESTART'
    if len(remote)==1:
        pid=int(remote[0][0])
        if pid==state.get('managed_pid'):
            if detected.get('socket') is False:
                if state.get('socket_suspect_count',0) >= SUSPECT_THRESHOLD:
                    return 'MANAGED_SOCKET_DEGRADED_REVIEW'
                return 'MANAGED_SOCKET_SUSPECT'
            return 'MANAGED_RUNNING'
        return 'EXTERNAL_AGENT_PRESENT_NO_DUPLICATE'
    if now_ts < state.get('cooldown_until',0):
        return 'COOLDOWN'
    recent=[t for t in state.get('restarts',[]) if t>now_ts-WINDOW_SECONDS]
    if len(recent)>=MAX_RESTARTS:
        return 'RESTART_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED'
    return 'START_REMOTE_AGENT'


def start_remote() -> tuple[int | None,str]:
    node=node_binary()
    script=remote_script()
    if not node or not script:
        return None,'MISSING_NODE_OR_VERIFIED_LOCAL_PACKAGE'
    with AGENT_LOG.open('ab',buffering=0) as log:
        proc=subprocess.Popen([str(node),str(script),'remote'],stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL,
                              stdout=log,stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
                              cwd=str(script.parent.parent),start_new_session=True)
    time.sleep(1.0)
    if proc.poll() is not None:
        return None,'REMOTE_AGENT_EXIT_'+str(proc.returncode)
    return proc.pid,'STARTED_EXISTING_PACKAGE'


def check_once(dry_run: bool=False, reachability: Callable=cloud_reachable,
               processes: Callable=process_rows) -> dict:
    ROOT.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True,mode=0o700)
    with LOCK.open('a+') as lf:
        fcntl.flock(lf,fcntl.LOCK_EX)
        state=load(STATE,{'created_at':iso(),'managed_pid':None,'restarts':[],
                          'socket_suspect_count':0})
        now_ts=time.time()
        rows=processes()
        observed=owner_processes(rows)
        observed['engineering_pids']=active_engineering_processes(rows)
        observed['laya_hook_timeout_count']=laya_timeout_count()
        if len(observed['remote'])==1:
            observed['socket']=outgoing_socket_present(observed['remote'][0][0])
        else:
            observed['socket']=None
        if observed['socket'] is False:
            state['socket_suspect_count']=state.get('socket_suspect_count',0)+1
        else:
            state['socket_suspect_count']=0
        cloud_ok,cloud_reason=reachability()
        action=choose_action(state,observed,cloud_ok,now_ts)
        decision=action
        if action=='START_REMOTE_AGENT' and not dry_run:
            pid,reason=start_remote()
            if pid:
                state['managed_pid']=pid
                state['restarts']=[t for t in state.get('restarts',[]) if t>now_ts-WINDOW_SECONDS]+[now_ts]
                state['cooldown_until']=now_ts+COOLDOWN_SECONDS
                decision='STARTED_REMOTE_AGENT'
            else:
                state['cooldown_until']=now_ts+COOLDOWN_SECONDS
                decision=reason
        elif dry_run and action=='START_REMOTE_AGENT':
            decision='WOULD_START_REMOTE_AGENT'
        observed.pop('remote',None)
        # No full command lines or tokens in logs, only PIDs and state.
        state['last_check_at']=iso()
        state['last_decision']=decision
        state['observed']={'remote_pids':[pid for pid,_ in owner_processes(rows)['remote']],
                           'laya_bridge_pids':observed['laya_bridge_pids'],
                           'laya_hook_timeout_count':observed['laya_hook_timeout_count'],
                           'engineering_pids':observed['engineering_pids'],
                           'cloud_tls':cloud_reason,'cloud_ok':cloud_ok,
                           'outgoing_socket':observed['socket']}
        if decision != state.get('last_event_decision'):
            event('STATUS_TRANSITION',{'from':state.get('last_event_decision'),
                                       'to':decision,'observed':state['observed']})
            state['last_event_decision']=decision
        write_atomic(STATE,state)
        return {'decision':decision,**state['observed'],'checked_at':state['last_check_at']}


def main():
    parser=argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--dry-run',action='store_true')
    parser.add_argument('--status',action='store_true')
    args=parser.parse_args()
    if args.status:
        print(json.dumps(load(STATE,{'status':'NOT_RUN'}),sort_keys=True,indent=2))
        return
    out=check_once(dry_run=args.dry_run)
    print(json.dumps(out,sort_keys=True))

if __name__=='__main__':
    main()

import importlib.util
import pathlib
import sys
import tempfile
import unittest
from unittest import mock

SRC = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]/'guardian.py'
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('guardian', SRC)
agent = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
sys.modules['guardian'] = agent
spec.loader.exec_module(agent)

class RemoteGuardTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def base(self, **kw):
        v={'remote':[], 'laya_bridge_count':0, 'laya_bridge_pids':[],
           'engineering_pids':[], 'laya_hook_timeout_count':0,'socket':None}
        v.update(kw)
        return v

    def test_absent_agent_starts(self):
        self.assertEqual(agent.choose_action({}, self.base(), True, 1000), 'START_REMOTE_AGENT')

    def test_offline_cloud_does_not_restart(self):
        self.assertEqual(agent.choose_action({}, self.base(), False, 1000), 'NETWORK_DEGRADED_NO_RESTART')

    def test_existing_manual_agent_not_killed_or_duplicated(self):
        self.assertEqual(agent.choose_action({'managed_pid':12}, self.base(remote=[(32,'node ...')]), True,1000),
                         'EXTERNAL_AGENT_PRESENT_NO_DUPLICATE')

    def test_managed_agent_running(self):
        self.assertEqual(agent.choose_action({'managed_pid':32}, self.base(remote=[(32,'node ...')],socket=True),True,1000),
                         'MANAGED_RUNNING')

    def test_no_disruption_on_transient_unhealthy_socket(self):
        self.assertEqual(agent.choose_action({'managed_pid':32,'socket_suspect_count':1},
                                             self.base(remote=[(32,'node ...')],socket=False),True,1000),
                         'MANAGED_SOCKET_SUSPECT')

    def test_degraded_agent_recycles_only_after_multiple_checks(self):
        self.assertEqual(agent.choose_action({'managed_pid':32,'socket_suspect_count':3},
                                             self.base(remote=[(32,'node ...')],socket=False),True,1000),
                         'RECYCLE_MANAGED_AGENT')

    def test_crash_loop_cooldown(self):
        self.assertEqual(agent.choose_action({'cooldown_until':1100},self.base(), True,1000),'COOLDOWN')
        self.assertEqual(agent.choose_action({'restarts':[910,925,950]},self.base(), True,1000),
                         'RESTART_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED')

    def test_matching_targets_remote_node_only(self):
        self.assertTrue(agent.is_remote_process('node /home/test/node_modules/@wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander/dist/index.js remote'))
        self.assertFalse(agent.is_remote_process('node /home/test/node_modules/@wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander/dist/index.js'))
        self.assertFalse(agent.is_remote_process('python3 guardian.py --dry-run'))
        self.assertFalse(agent.is_remote_process('npx remote other package'))

    def test_identifies_existing_laya_sidecars(self):
        rows=[(100,'node /usr/local/node_modules/@wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander/dist/index.js remote'),
              (101,'python /Users/user/.omp/plugins/node_modules/omp-laya-judge/server/bridge.py'),
              (102,'python unrelated.py')]
        observed=agent.owner_processes(rows)
        self.assertEqual(observed['laya_bridge_count'],1)
        self.assertEqual(observed['remote'][0][0],100)

    def test_dry_run_does_not_spawn(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            with mock.patch.object(agent,'ROOT',pathlib.Path(tmp)), \
                 mock.patch.object(agent,'STATE',pathlib.Path(tmp)/'state.json'), \
                 mock.patch.object(agent,'EVENTS',pathlib.Path(tmp)/'events.jsonl'), \
                 mock.patch.object(agent,'LOCK',pathlib.Path(tmp)/'.lock'), \

#!/bin/bash
# GMRI Remote Device Resilience -- install as a per-user macOS LaunchAgent.
# Does not change network settings, grant tool permissions, or delete credentials.
set -euo pipefail
HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
if [[ "$(uname -s)" != "Darwin" ]]; then
  echo "This installer runs on the Mac only."
  exit 2
fi
PY=""
for CAND in "$HOME/.local/bin/python3" /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 /usr/local/bin/python3 /usr/bin/python3; do
  if [[ -x "$CAND" ]]; then PY="$CAND"; break; fi
done
if [[ -z "$PY" ]]; then echo "Python 3 required; nothing changed."; exit 2; fi
TARGET="$HOME/.gmri/remote-guardian"
PLIST="$HOME/Library/LaunchAgents/org.grizzlymedicine.remote-guardian.plist"
mkdir -p "$TARGET" "$HOME/Library/LaunchAgents"
chmod 700 "$TARGET"
# Preflight the candidate before replacing any existing guardian.
"$PY" -m py_compile "$HERE/guardian.py"
if [[ -f "$TARGET/guardian.py" ]]; then
  cp "$TARGET/guardian.py" "$TARGET/guardian.py.backup-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)"
fi
cp "$HERE/guardian.py" "$TARGET/guardian.py"
chmod 700 "$TARGET/guardian.py"
"$PY" - "$PY" "$TARGET" "$PLIST" <<'PY'
import pathlib, plistlib, sys
python, target, plist = sys.argv[1:]
root=pathlib.Path(target)
contents={
  'Label':'org.grizzlymedicine.remote-guardian',
  'ProgramArguments':[python,str(root/'guardian.py')],
  'WorkingDirectory':str(root),
  'RunAtLoad':True,
  'StartInterval':90,
  'StandardOutPath':str(root/'launchd.stdout.log'),
  'StandardErrorPath':str(root/'launchd.stderr.log'),
  'ProcessType':'Background',
  'Nice':10,
}
p=pathlib.Path(plist)
if p.exists():
    backup=p.with_name(p.name+'.backup')
    backup.write_bytes(p.read_bytes())
p.write_bytes(plistlib.dumps(contents,sort_keys=True))
PY
chmod 600 "$PLIST"
/usr/bin/plutil -lint "$PLIST"
ID="$(id -u)"
LABEL='org.grizzlymedicine.remote-guardian'
# Re-bootstrap only this new guardian service on reinstall; no other agent is touched.
/bin/launchctl bootout "gui/$ID/$LABEL" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
/bin/launchctl bootstrap "gui/$ID" "$PLIST"
/bin/launchctl kickstart "gui/$ID/$LABEL"
echo "Installed GMRI remote guardian: interval 90 seconds."

# GMRI Remote Recovery — 8 October 2026

**Purpose:** Keep the authorized Desktop Commander *remote device* connected when its terminal or local Node agent exits; diagnose transient link failures and nearby L-A-Y-A hook timeouts without touching the operating system's sleep settings, user recordings, Proxmox disks, or OMP approval policy.

**Installation:** On the authenticated MacBook, extract the ZIP and run `Install.command` (right-click **Open** if macOS warns about an unsigned local script). This installs a **per-user LaunchAgent** that runs every 90 seconds. Existing terminal-controlled Desktop Commander agents are left running; the guardian takes over only after an agent exits or a subsequently guardian-owned agent loses its external TCP connection repeatedly.

**Actions and boundaries**

- Detect running Desktop Commander Remote and L-A-Y-A Python bridge PIDs. Do not log environment variables or auth tokens.
- Check outbound HTTPS/TLS to the official remote provider independently of a local process check. TLS availability alone does *not* prove device registration/authorization.
- If no remote agent exists and the cloud is reachable, restart using the exact locally installed `@wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander` code and **existing saved OAuth credentials**, never an online `npx @latest` update.
- Avoid creating duplicates while the agent already runs in a Terminal. Never kill terminal-owned agents. A guardian-managed agent may receive a targeted SIGTERM only after three consecutive 90-second polls with no observed external TCP connection; the next check may re-launch after its cooldown.
- Maximum three successful starts per 30 minutes; 180-second post-launch cooldown. No credential reset, broad process kill, privilege escalation, firewall changes, system reboot, or sleep settings modification.
- Collect bounded L-A-Y-A pre-hook timeout counts from the specific GMRI OMP coordinator logs. This flags engineering stalls **but does not claim to fix L-A-Y-A's internal 30-second hook behavior** or give an LLM unconstrained shell authority. The watchdog does not depend on L-A-Y-A to remain available.
- Retain append-only change-of-state receipts, plus an atomic state snapshot in `~/.gmri/remote-guardian/`.

**Important limitation:** There is no provider-sanctioned local endpoint for confirming whether the *ChatGPT cloud UI* can actually route a tool call to this device; the guardian monitors process health, outbound TCP, TLS availability, and reconnection attempts. It cannot repair a ChatGPT backend `The request timed out` incident. Desktop Commander account revocation also requires operator reauthorization; it will not blindly clear credentials.

**Check status:** `python3 ~/.gmri/remote-guardian/guardian.py --status`.

**Disable/roll back:** Run `Uninstall.command`. Evidence and the Desktop Commander authenticated device session are retained.

**Installation status in ChatGPT:** A generated package is **not** evidence that it has been installed on the user's Mac. Confirmation requires successful installer invocation and a working remote status check.
MD

#!/bin/bash
# GMRI final-push repair: resilient engineering supervisor and Desktop Commander reattachment.
# Scoped to ~/.gmri and existing GMRI Oct 8 director files. No production VM/container mutation.
set -euo pipefail
umask 077

if [[ "$(uname -s)" != "Darwin" ]]; then
  echo 'ERROR: Run this script on the GMRI Mac (macOS), not on Proxmox.' >&2
  exit 2
fi

DIRECTOR="$BASE/director.py"
STATE="$BASE/director_state.json"

if [[ ! -f "$DIRECTOR" || ! -f "$STATE" || ! -f "$AGENT" ]]; then
  echo 'ERROR: Existing Oct 8 director installation missing; no changes made.' >&2
  exit 2
fi

if [[ ! -x /opt/homebrew/bin/npx && ! -x /usr/local/bin/npx ]]; then
  echo 'ERROR: No installed npx binary; cannot activate remote reconnect.' >&2

# Fail closed if the installed source does not match the known failure-causing branch.
# The Python tool holds the SAME fcntl lock as director.py and makes a backup.
/usr/bin/python3 - "$DIRECTOR" "$STATE" <<'PY'
import ast, datetime, fcntl, json, os, pathlib, shutil, sys, tempfile
src_path, state_path = [pathlib.Path(s) for s in sys.argv[1:3]]
base = src_path.parent
lock_path=base/'.director.lock'
with lock_path.open('a+') as lock:
    fcntl.flock(lock, fcntl.LOCK_EX)
    orig=src_path.read_text()
    current=orig
    stamps=datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).strftime('%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ')

    old_remote='''    if remote_error:
        current["last_remote_error"] = remote_error
        current["phase"] = "REMOTE_STATE_UNAVAILABLE_NO_LAUNCH"
        atomic(STATE, current)
        return current
    current.pop("last_remote_error", None)'''
    new_remote='''    # Remote PVE event-ledger loss is degraded observability, NOT a reason to
    # freeze all local engineering. Each worker must still reconcile its own
    # durable mission and live effects before doing a consequential mutation.
    if remote_error:
        current["last_remote_error"] = remote_error
        current["remote_observability"] = "DEGRADED"
    else:
        current.pop("last_remote_error", None)
        current["remote_observability"] = "OK"'''
    if old_remote in current:
        current=current.replace(old_remote,new_remote,1)
    elif new_remote not in current:
        raise RuntimeError('Director remote-state branch differs; refusing unsafe blind patch')

    old_early='''                if w["rapid_exits"] >= 2:
                    w["held"] = "TWO_EARLY_EXITS_NEED_DIAGNOSIS"
                    notify(info["status_key"], "BLOCKED",
                           "Engineering worker stopped early twice; review local logs and restart cause.",
                           BASE / "director_state.json")
                    continue'''
    new_early='''                if w["rapid_exits"] >= 2:
                    # Bounded exponential backoff, instead of a permanent dead-end.
                    # Keeps work alive through transient provider/network errors.
                    wait_s = min(900, 60 * (2 ** min(w["rapid_exits"] - 2, 4)))
                    if runtime < wait_s:
                        w["state"] = "RETRY_BACKOFF"
                        w["retry_after_seconds"] = max(1, int(wait_s - runtime))
                        continue'''
    if old_early in current:
        current=current.replace(old_early,new_early,1)
    elif new_early not in current:
        raise RuntimeError('Director early-exit branch differs; refusing unsafe blind patch')

    old_budget='''        if w.get("rounds", 0) >= 8:
            w["held"] = "RESTART_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED"
            continue'''
    new_budget='''        if w.get("rounds", 0) >= 80:
            w["held"] = "RESTART_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED"
            continue'''
    if old_budget in current:
        current=current.replace(old_budget,new_budget,1)
    elif new_budget not in current:
        raise RuntimeError('Director restart-budget branch differs; refusing unsafe blind patch')

    # Prevent an old permanent rapid-exit hold from defeating the repaired backoff.
    old_hold='''        if w.get("completed") or w.get("held"):
            continue'''
    new_hold='''        if w.get("completed"):
            continue
        if w.get("held"):
            continue'''
    if old_hold in current:
        current=current.replace(old_hold,new_hold,1)

    ast.parse(current, filename=str(src_path))
    data=json.loads(state_path.read_text())
    before=base/(f'director-before-recovery-{stamps}.py')
    before_state=base/(f'director-state-before-recovery-{stamps}.json')
    shutil.copy2(src_path,before)
    shutil.copy2(state_path,before_state)
    for name,worker in data.get('workers',{}).items():
        if worker.get('held')=='TWO_EARLY_EXITS_NEED_DIAGNOSIS':
            worker['held']=None
            worker['rapid_exits']=0
            worker['state']='NOT_RUNNING'
            worker['recovery_override']={
                'time':datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat(),
                'reason':'permanent rapid-exit lockout replaced with bounded backoff',
                'previous':str(before_state)
            }
    data.setdefault('recovery_history',[]).append({
       'time': datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat(),
       'scope':'supervisor_remote_state_nonblocking_and_bounded_restart',
       'source_backup':str(before),
       'state_backup':str(before_state)
    })
    def write_atomic(path, content):
        fd,temp=tempfile.mkstemp(prefix='.gmri-recovery-',dir=path.parent)
        try:
            with os.fdopen(fd,'w') as f:
                f.write(content)
                f.flush()
                os.fsync(f.fileno())
            os.replace(temp,path)
        finally:
            if os.path.exists(temp): os.unlink(temp)

    write_atomic(state_path,json.dumps(data,sort_keys=True,indent=2)+'\n')

[L2]   "content": "---\nname: macos-harness\ndescription: Control a whole Mac from one persistent Python session with screenshots, PID-targeted input, an animated virtual pointer, targeted Apple Accessibility, Apple Events, Browser Harness CDP, and filesystem access. Use for native, Electron, browser, dialog, file, or cross-app tasks without moving the physical cursor or forcing apps into the foreground.\n---\n\n# macOS Harness\n\nUse one CLI call per decision point, not per primitive:\n\n```bash\nmacos-harness <<'PY'\napp = \"Spotify\"\nmac.see(app)\nmac.key(\"cmd+k\", app=app)\nmac.type(\"Alessia Cara\", app=app)\nprint(mac.see(app))\nPY\n```\n\nThe CLI preloads `mac`, `browser`, `Path`, and `subprocess`. Prefer bounded stdin\nprograms; reserve `macos-harness repl` for manual exploration and always exit it.\n\n## Minimize round trips\n\n- Bundle deterministic, reversible steps into one program, then verify once. Opening\n  search, typing a query, and capturing the results is one burst—not three calls.\n- Stop at a genuine decision boundary: ambiguous identity, new coordinates, an\n  irreversible action, or unexpected state. Inspect once, then run the next burst.\n- Do not screenshot merely to confirm that a known shortcut opened a text field\n  before typing. Let the final screenshot verify the whole sequence.\n- Poll exact AX or Apple Events state inside the same Python program when possible;\n  do not make the LLM repeatedly ask whether a transition finished.\n- Use the cheapest strong end-state check. Prefer one screenshot for visible state\n  or one exact API/AX query for semantic state; use both only when they prove\n  different things.\n\n## Use the small surface\n\nThink in six verbs: `see`, `key`, `type`, `click`, `ax`, `script`.\n\n```python\nframe = mac.see(\"Spotify\")\nmac.key(\"cmd+k\", app=\"Spotify\")\nmac.type(\"Alessia Cara\", app=\"Spotify\")\nmac.click(640, 420, app=\"Spotify\")\n\nitem = mac.ax.at(640, 420, app=\"Spotify\")\nmac.ax.perform(item[\"element_index\"], \"AXPress\")\n\nmac.script('tell application \"Spotify\" to play')\n```\n\nUse ordinary Python for local context and one-off logic. Do not add app-specific\nhelpers when a short program can resolve the task.\n\n## Choose the lowest useful mode\n\n1. When identity depends on local context (`my`, `friend`, or prior activity),\n   inspect that context and correlate stable fields; a loose text hit is not enough.\n2. Use `mac.script()` for a known exact, focus-safe app command.\n3. Otherwise use `mac.see(app)` and vision.\n4. Prefer a known keyboard route; use a verified coordinate for a visible,\n   low-risk target.\n5. Use targeted `mac.ax` only when semantic identity or state matters. Do not dump\n   a full AX tree before trying the direct route.\n\nAfter a failed verified burst, switch mode or stop. Never repair uncertainty with\nrepeated keys, clicks, deletion loops, or bulk input.\n\n## Keep the invariants\n\n- Input targets an already-running app PID and never requests activation or raise.\n- A background target becoming frontmost raises `FocusChangedError`; never\n  manipulate focus to restore it.\n- `mac.click()` is raw PID-targeted input. It never guesses an AX action.\n- The animated pointer is click-through and never moves the physical cursor.\n- `mac.move()` moves only that pointer; it cannot produce native hover.\n- Inactive apps may reject raw clicks. After one verified failure, switch mode.\n- Never launch a closed app or use a custom URL scheme when focus is forbidden.\n- Screenshot coordinates come from the latest `mac.see()` and preserve window\n  bounds and Retina scaling.\n\nSecondary primitives are `mac.move`, `drag`, `scroll`, `show_pointer`, and\n`hide_pointer`. `mac.ax.query()` returns compact matches and bounds fallback\ntraversal; lower `max_nodes` for especially large apps.\n\n## Browser and permissions\n\nUse `browser` for DOM, tabs, network, downloads, and uploads. Do not substitute AX\nfor CDP inside a web page. While Browser Harness connects, macOS Harness accepts\nChrome's exact `Allow remote debugging?` sheet through system-wide AX. It never\nactivates Chrome or emits a mouse event.\n\nRun `macos-harness doctor` to inspect permissions without prompting. Run\n`macos-harness doctor --request` only with user approval. Accessibility, screen\nrecording, and event posting are global; Apple Events Automation is per target.\n",
